blocks.text: Genesis 5 opens by recalling that humanity was made in God’s likeness, then describes Seth as a son in Adam’s likeness and image. From there, a repeated formula—age when a son is fathered, additional years lived, total lifespan, and a closing notice—organizes the line from Adam toward Noah. Within that regular structure, the recurring words “and he died” form a pronounced refrain of mortality.

The genealogy does more than preserve names and ages: it maintains an unbroken narrative line from Adam to Noah while developing the chapter’s themes of mortality and hope. Enoch notably interrupts the usual death formula; instead of “and he died,” the text says that he walked with God and that God took him. At the chapter’s end, Lamech names Noah in hope that he will bring relief from labor on the cursed ground. On this reading, the genealogy functions as narrative and thematic development rather than presenting itself explicitly as a modern chronology table.

Genesis 5 belongs within the ancient theological and literary discourse of Genesis 1–11. That setting cautions against forcing the chapter into a modern scientific genre or dismissing it as merely decorative myth. Comparisons with other ancient Near Eastern traditions may illuminate shared motifs and cultural questions, but similarities by themselves neither prove direct copying nor settle how Genesis should be interpreted.
